title: LEAD
description: LEAD(column) OVER (...) is LAG's mirror image - it reaches FORWARD to a following row instead of back. Write a query that returns each order's `customer_id`, `order_date`, and that SAME customer's NEXT order_date (NULL if it's their most recent order), using LEAD.
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: LEAD, window function

Same PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date setup as LAG - the only difference is which direction you look. LEAD(order_date) OVER (...) reads the NEXT row's order_date instead of the previous one.
Select customer_id, order_date, and a LEAD(order_date) window function partitioned by customer_id and ordered by order_date, from orders.
expected_behavior: Returns customer_id, order_date, and next_order_date (NULL for each customer's most recent order, chronologically).
solution: SELECT customer_id, order_date, LEAD(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS next_order_date FROM orders;
explanation: LAG and LEAD together let you compute row-to-row differences (like "days since the last order") entirely in SQL, without pulling the data out and comparing rows in application code.
